Antibiotic classes: when to use, usual doses, side effects

Hospitalist Toolkit · Antibiotics tab · adults · one class per page
Decision-support draft, not verified. Written by Claude from general knowledge. Doses are typical adult doses for normal kidney and liver function; renal column = needs adjustment. Always check the Island Health formulary, pharmacy, local antibiogram and allergy history. Choose the narrowest drug that covers the likely or proven organism.

Before you prescribe

  • Send cultures first when it does not delay treatment of sepsis.
  • Write the indication and the planned stop date or review date on the order.
  • Reassess at 48–72 h: narrow to the organism, switch IV to PO, stop if not infection.
  • Short courses work for most infections: CAP 5 days, cystitis 3–5, pyelonephritis 7 (FQ) –10, cellulitis 5–6, uncomplicated gram-negative bacteremia 7, intra-abdominal after source control 4.

Penicillins

Pen G/V, amoxicillin, amox-clav, ampicillin, cloxacillin, piperacillin-tazobactam
CoversStrep, enterococcus (amp/amox), MSSA (cloxacillin, amox-clav), anaerobes (amox-clav, pip-tazo), Pseudomonas (pip-tazo only)
Does not coverMRSA, atypicals; ESBL (pip-tazo unreliable for ESBL bacteremia – MERINO)

When to use

  • Strep pyogenes (pharyngitis, cellulitis, necrotizing infection with clindamycin), syphilis, susceptible strep endocarditis → penicillin G
  • Enterococcus faecalis, Listeria → ampicillin
  • MSSA bacteremia/endocarditis/osteomyelitis → cloxacillin (or cefazolin)
  • Bites, aspiration, sinusitis, COPD exacerbation, step-down for intra-abdominal infection → amoxicillin-clavulanate
  • Hospital-acquired / Pseudomonas risk / febrile neutropenia / severe intra-abdominal → piperacillin-tazobactam

Usual adult doses

AgentUsual dose (normal renal function)Renal adjust?
Penicillin G (IV)2–4 million units IV q4h (4 MU q4h for endocarditis, meningitis, neurosyphilis)Yes
Penicillin V (PO)300–600 mg PO QID (strep pharyngitis 600 mg BID ×10 days)Yes
Amoxicillin500 mg–1 g PO TID (CAP 1 g TID)Yes
Amoxicillin-clavulanate875/125 mg PO BID (or 500/125 mg TID)Yes
Ampicillin1–2 g IV q4–6h (2 g q4h for enterococcal endocarditis, Listeria)Yes
Cloxacillin2 g IV q4h (MSSA bacteremia); 500 mg PO QID (poor oral absorption – prefer cephalexin PO)No
Piperacillin-tazobactam4.5 g IV q6–8h (q6h or extended infusion for Pseudomonas / severe sepsis)Yes

Side effects and interactions

  • Hypersensitivity: rash, urticaria, anaphylaxis, rarely SJS/TEN/DRESS
  • Diarrhea, C. difficile (amox-clav, pip-tazo)
  • Interstitial nephritis; neutropenia and drug fever with long courses (>2 weeks)
  • Seizures with high doses in renal failure
  • Hypokalemia and sodium load (pip-tazo); AKI more often with vancomycin + pip-tazo
  • Amox-clav: cholestatic hepatitis (older men, longer courses)

Monitoring / pearls

CBC and creatinine weekly on long IV courses (OPAT). Amoxicillin rash in EBV infection is not a true allergy.

Cephalosporins

Cefazolin, cephalexin, cefuroxime, ceftriaxone, ceftazidime, cefepime, ceftaroline
Covers1st gen: MSSA, strep, E. coli. 3rd gen: gram-negatives, pneumococcus, meningitis. Ceftazidime/cefepime: Pseudomonas. Ceftaroline: MRSA
Does not coverEnterococcus (none), Listeria, atypicals, anaerobes (poor), ESBL/AmpC producers

When to use

  • Cellulitis, MSSA bacteremia, surgical prophylaxis → cefazolin (PO step-down cephalexin)
  • Community-acquired pneumonia (with macrolide/doxy), pyelonephritis, SBP, meningitis, gonorrhea → ceftriaxone
  • Pseudomonas, febrile neutropenia, hospital-acquired pneumonia → cefepime or ceftazidime
  • MRSA when vancomycin is not suitable → ceftaroline (ID input)
  • Ceftazidime-avibactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam → MDR Pseudomonas / CRE: ID approval only

Usual adult doses

AgentUsual dose (normal renal function)Renal adjust?
Cefazolin1–2 g IV q8h (2 g q8h for MSSA bacteremia; 3 g if ≥120 kg for surgical prophylaxis)Yes
Cephalexin500 mg–1 g PO QIDYes
Cefuroxime750 mg–1.5 g IV q8h; axetil 500 mg PO BIDYes
Ceftriaxone1–2 g IV q24h (meningitis 2 g IV q12h; gonorrhea 500 mg–1 g IM once)No
Cefixime400 mg PO dailyYes
Ceftazidime1–2 g IV q8h (2 g q8h for Pseudomonas)Yes
Cefepime1–2 g IV q8–12h (2 g q8h for febrile neutropenia / Pseudomonas)Yes – neurotoxicity
Ceftaroline600 mg IV q12h (q8h for severe MRSA)Yes

Side effects and interactions

  • Hypersensitivity; cross-reactivity with penicillin ~1–2%, mostly through shared side chains (cephalexin/cefadroxil with amoxicillin/ampicillin; ceftazidime with aztreonam)
  • C. difficile (3rd generation especially)
  • Cefepime neurotoxicity: confusion, myoclonus, non-convulsive status – mainly when not renally dosed
  • Ceftriaxone: biliary sludge/pseudolithiasis, immune hemolysis (rare)
  • Cytopenias, interstitial nephritis, drug fever with long courses

Monitoring / pearls

Cefepime: dose to CrCl; think of it in a confused patient with kidney disease. Ceftriaxone needs no renal adjustment.

Carbapenems and aztreonam

Meropenem, ertapenem, imipenem-cilastatin; aztreonam (monobactam)
CoversBroadest beta-lactams: gram-negatives incl. ESBL, anaerobes, strep, MSSA. Meropenem/imipenem: Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter. Aztreonam: gram-negatives incl. Pseudomonas only
Does not coverMRSA, E. faecium (VRE), Stenotrophomonas, atypicals; ertapenem misses Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, enterococcus; aztreonam has no gram-positive or anaerobe cover

When to use

  • ESBL-producing Enterobacterales infection (bacteremia, pyelonephritis) → ertapenem (no Pseudomonas risk) or meropenem
  • Severe hospital-acquired sepsis, febrile neutropenia with previous resistant organisms, CNS infection with resistant gram-negatives → meropenem
  • Severe penicillin allergy needing gram-negative/Pseudomonas cover → aztreonam (avoid if ceftazidime allergy)
  • Carbapenem-sparing: de-escalate as soon as susceptibilities return

Usual adult doses

AgentUsual dose (normal renal function)Renal adjust?
Meropenem1 g IV q8h (2 g q8h for meningitis, Pseudomonas, severe infection; extended infusion)Yes
Ertapenem1 g IV q24hYes (500 mg if CrCl <30)
Imipenem-cilastatin500 mg IV q6hYes
Aztreonam1–2 g IV q8h (2 g q6–8h for Pseudomonas)Yes

Side effects and interactions

  • Seizures (imipenem > meropenem/ertapenem), especially renal failure or CNS disease
  • Valproate interaction: carbapenems cut valproate levels within a day → breakthrough seizures. Avoid together; use another antibiotic or another antiseizure drug
  • C. difficile; selects for carbapenem-resistant organisms
  • Hypersensitivity: cross-reactivity with penicillin <1%
  • Aztreonam: rash, LFT rise; safe in most beta-lactam allergy

Monitoring / pearls

Check the medication list for valproate before starting. Reserve meropenem: ID / stewardship review at 48–72 h.

Anti-MRSA agents

Vancomycin, daptomycin, linezolid (plus TMP-SMX, doxycycline, ceftaroline on other pages)
CoversMRSA, MSSA (inferior to cloxacillin/cefazolin for MSSA), strep, enterococcus (vancomycin for amp-R; linezolid/daptomycin for VRE), C. difficile (oral vancomycin)
Does not coverAll gram-negatives

When to use

  • Sepsis with MRSA risk (known colonization, injection drug use, severe purulent SSTI, necrotizing pneumonia), empiric meningitis → IV vancomycin; stop at 48–72 h if no MRSA
  • MRSA bacteremia/endocarditis → vancomycin or daptomycin (high dose); ID consult for every S. aureus bacteremia
  • MRSA pneumonia → vancomycin or linezolid (not daptomycin)
  • VRE → linezolid or daptomycin
  • Gram-positive infection with severe beta-lactam allergy → vancomycin

Usual adult doses

AgentUsual dose (normal renal function)Renal adjust?
Vancomycin IVLoad 20–35 mg/kg (max ~3 g), then 15–20 mg/kg q8–12h; AUC 400–600 or trough per pharmacy protocolYes – levels
Vancomycin POC. difficile: 125 mg PO QID ×10 days (fulminant 500 mg QID) – not absorbed, no levelsNo
Daptomycin6 mg/kg IV q24h; 8–10 mg/kg for bacteremia/endocarditisYes (q48h if CrCl <30)
Linezolid600 mg PO/IV q12h (100% oral bioavailability)No
Rifampin (adjunct only)300–450 mg PO BID with another active drug for prosthetic material/hardware – never aloneNo

Side effects and interactions

  • Vancomycin: AKI (higher with pip-tazo, other nephrotoxins), infusion reaction (flushing – slow the infusion, not allergy), neutropenia, DRESS, ototoxicity (rare)
  • Daptomycin: CK rise/myopathy (check CK weekly; hold statins), eosinophilic pneumonia; inactivated by surfactant → no use in pneumonia
  • Linezolid: thrombocytopenia/anemia (>10–14 days), serotonin syndrome with SSRIs/SNRIs/MAOIs, lactic acidosis, hypoglycemia, peripheral and optic neuropathy with long courses
  • Rifampin: major CYP inducer (DOACs, warfarin, tacrolimus, azoles, opioids, contraceptives), orange body fluids, hepatitis

Monitoring / pearls

Vancomycin levels and creatinine 2–3×/week; daptomycin CK weekly; linezolid CBC weekly and review serotonergic drugs.

Aminoglycosides

Gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin
CoversAerobic gram-negatives incl. Pseudomonas (tobramycin best), synergy with beta-lactams for enterococcal/strep endocarditis
Does not coverAnaerobes, strep alone, MRSA alone; poor in abscess (acidic, low oxygen), poor lung and CNS penetration

When to use

  • One empiric dose for gram-negative sepsis or pyelonephritis while cultures pending (single doses carry little toxicity)
  • Pyelonephritis / complicated UTI with resistant organism and normal kidney function
  • Synergy: enterococcal endocarditis (gentamicin) – or ampicillin + ceftriaxone instead to avoid nephrotoxicity
  • Plague, tularemia; amikacin for some mycobacteria and MDR gram-negatives (ID)

Usual adult doses

AgentUsual dose (normal renal function)Renal adjust?
Gentamicin / tobramycin5–7 mg/kg IV q24h (extended interval; use adjusted body weight if obese)Yes – levels, interval
Gentamicin (synergy)1 mg/kg IV q8h (enterococcus) or 3 mg/kg q24h (viridans strep)Yes
Amikacin15–20 mg/kg IV q24hYes

Side effects and interactions

  • Nephrotoxicity (non-oliguric AKI, usually after 5–7 days; often reversible)
  • Ototoxicity: vestibular (imbalance, oscillopsia) and cochlear – often permanent
  • Neuromuscular blockade (myasthenia gravis, after anesthesia)
  • Worse with vancomycin, loop diuretics, contrast, NSAIDs, amphotericin

Monitoring / pearls

Avoid in CKD, older adults and >5–7 days where possible. Levels per pharmacy nomogram; creatinine every 2–3 days; ask about dizziness/tinnitus.

Hospitalist Toolkit · Antibiotics tab · antibiotic classes reference · page 6 · UNVERIFIED draft (Nov 2026)

Fluoroquinolones

Ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin
CoversGram-negatives incl. Pseudomonas (cipro, levo), atypicals (levo, moxi), pneumococcus (levo, moxi), anaerobes (moxi only)
Does not coverCipro: strep/pneumococcus poor. MRSA (unreliable), enterococcus (weak). Moxifloxacin: urinary infections (low urine levels), Pseudomonas

When to use

  • Pyelonephritis, complicated UTI, prostatitis (best prostate penetration) → ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin
  • Pseudomonas when an oral drug is needed → ciprofloxacin 750 mg BID
  • CAP with severe beta-lactam allergy → levofloxacin or moxifloxacin
  • Gram-negative bone/joint step-down; traveller's diarrhea
  • Health Canada warnings: avoid for uncomplicated cystitis, sinusitis and bronchitis when alternatives exist

Usual adult doses

AgentUsual dose (normal renal function)Renal adjust?
Ciprofloxacin500–750 mg PO BID; 400 mg IV q8–12hYes
Levofloxacin750 mg PO/IV daily (500 mg for some UTI)Yes
Moxifloxacin400 mg PO/IV dailyNo

Side effects and interactions

  • QT prolongation (moxi > levo > cipro) – check ECG with other QT drugs, low K/Mg
  • Tendinopathy/rupture (age >60, steroids, transplant), aortic aneurysm/dissection
  • Dysglycemia (hypo- and hyperglycemia), especially diabetics on insulin/sulfonylureas
  • CNS: delirium, insomnia, seizures; peripheral neuropathy (may be permanent)
  • C. difficile, photosensitivity, myasthenia gravis worsening
  • Chelation: separate from Ca, Mg, Al, Fe, Zn and enteral feeds (give FQ 2 h before or 6 h after); warfarin INR rises

Monitoring / pearls

100% oral bioavailability – IV rarely needed. Review QTc and co-prescribed QT drugs.

Macrolides and tetracyclines

Azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin; doxycycline, minocycline, tigecycline
CoversAtypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Legionella), pneumococcus (rising resistance), H. influenzae/Moraxella. Doxycycline also: MRSA (SSTI), Rickettsia, Lyme, Leptospira, chlamydia
Does not coverMost gram-negative rods, Pseudomonas, enterococcus; macrolides not for S. aureus; tigecycline poor serum levels (not for bacteremia) and no Pseudomonas

When to use

  • CAP: atypical cover with a beta-lactam (azithromycin or doxycycline); outpatient CAP without comorbidities → doxycycline or amoxicillin
  • COPD exacerbation (doxycycline); chronic azithromycin to reduce COPD exacerbations/bronchiectasis
  • Chlamydia, pertussis, Campylobacter, traveller's diarrhea (azithromycin)
  • MRSA SSTI step-down, Lyme, tick-borne illness (doxycycline)
  • H. pylori, MAC (clarithromycin); erythromycin IV as a prokinetic (gastroparesis, before endoscopy for upper GI bleed)

Usual adult doses

AgentUsual dose (normal renal function)Renal adjust?
Azithromycin500 mg PO/IV daily ×3 days (or 500 mg day 1 then 250 mg ×4); chlamydia 1 g onceNo
Clarithromycin500 mg PO BIDYes
Erythromycin (prokinetic)250 mg IV 30–90 min before endoscopy; 125–250 mg PO TID-QID for gastroparesis (short term)No
Doxycycline100 mg PO/IV BID (200 mg first dose)No
Minocycline100 mg PO BIDNo
Tigecycline100 mg IV once, then 50 mg q12h (reserve, ID)No (hepatic)

Side effects and interactions

  • QT prolongation (azithro, clarithro, erythro); GI upset; hepatotoxicity; hearing loss (high dose)
  • Clarithromycin/erythromycin: strong CYP3A4 inhibitors – statins (rhabdo), colchicine (toxicity), DOACs, calcium channel blockers, tacrolimus, cyclosporine; azithromycin has few interactions
  • Doxycycline: pill esophagitis (take upright with a full glass of water), photosensitivity, chelation with Ca/Fe/antacids; avoid in pregnancy
  • Minocycline: dizziness/vertigo, DRESS, drug-induced lupus, skin pigmentation
  • Tigecycline: nausea/vomiting, pancreatitis, higher all-cause mortality warning

Monitoring / pearls

Baseline QTc if other QT drugs; review interactions for clarithromycin. Doxycycline and minocycline need no renal adjustment.

Sulfonamide and urinary agents

TMP-SMX, trimethoprim, nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin
CoversTMP-SMX: E. coli/Enterobacterales (resistance often 20%+), MRSA, Stenotrophomonas, Nocardia, PJP, Toxoplasma. Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin: lower-tract E. coli incl. many ESBL, E. faecalis (nitrofurantoin)
Does not coverTMP-SMX: strep (cellulitis – add cephalexin), Pseudomonas, anaerobes. Nitrofurantoin/fosfomycin: no tissue or blood levels – not for pyelonephritis, prostatitis, bacteremia

When to use

  • Uncomplicated cystitis → nitrofurantoin 5 days, fosfomycin once, or TMP-SMX 3 days (if local resistance <20%)
  • Pyelonephritis/complicated UTI step-down when susceptible → TMP-SMX
  • Purulent SSTI/MRSA (often with cephalexin for strep), Stenotrophomonas → TMP-SMX
  • PJP treatment and prophylaxis (steroids ≥20 mg prednisone >4 weeks, transplant, HIV CD4 <200) → TMP-SMX
  • ESBL cystitis → fosfomycin or nitrofurantoin

Usual adult doses

AgentUsual dose (normal renal function)Renal adjust?
TMP-SMXUTI/SSTI 1 DS (160/800 mg) PO BID; larger patients/MRSA 2 DS BIDYes
TMP-SMX (PJP)Treatment 15–20 mg/kg/day TMP divided q6–8h; prophylaxis 1 SS daily or 1 DS 3×/weekYes
Trimethoprim100 mg PO BID or 200 mg dailyYes
Nitrofurantoin (Macrobid)100 mg PO BID ×5 daysAvoid if CrCl <30
Fosfomycin3 g PO once (sachet in water); some use 3 g q48–72h ×3 doses for complicated cystitisCaution

Side effects and interactions

  • TMP-SMX: hyperkalemia (with ACEi/ARB/spironolactone, CKD, elderly), creatinine rise without true GFR fall, rash → SJS/TEN, cytopenias, hepatitis, hypoglycemia with sulfonylureas, warfarin INR rises sharply, aseptic meningitis
  • Nitrofurantoin: acute pulmonary reaction (fever, dyspnea) and chronic pulmonary fibrosis with long use, hepatitis, peripheral neuropathy, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency
  • Fosfomycin: diarrhea, nausea

Monitoring / pearls

TMP-SMX: K and creatinine at day 3–5 in at-risk patients, INR if on warfarin, CBC on long courses.

Clindamycin and metronidazole

Clindamycin; metronidazole
CoversClindamycin: strep, MSSA, many MRSA (check D-test), anaerobes above the diaphragm, toxin suppression. Metronidazole: anaerobes (incl. B. fragilis, C. difficile), Trichomonas, Giardia, amoeba
Does not coverBoth: no aerobic gram-negatives. Clindamycin: B. fragilis resistance common, enterococcus. Metronidazole: no aerobes, no gram-positive aerobes

When to use

  • Necrotizing fasciitis, toxic shock (with a beta-lactam) → clindamycin to switch off toxin production
  • Cellulitis, dental infections, bone infection in beta-lactam allergy → clindamycin
  • Intra-abdominal infection (with ceftriaxone or a fluoroquinolone), aspiration with abscess, brain abscess → metronidazole
  • C. difficile only if oral vancomycin and fidaxomicin are unavailable (non-severe); fulminant C. difficile → IV metronidazole + oral vancomycin
  • Bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, amoebiasis, Giardia → metronidazole

Usual adult doses

AgentUsual dose (normal renal function)Renal adjust?
Clindamycin300–450 mg PO QID; 600–900 mg IV q8hNo
Metronidazole500 mg PO/IV q12h (q8h in some protocols); BV 500 mg PO BID ×7 daysNo (reduce in severe liver disease)

Side effects and interactions

  • Clindamycin: highest C. difficile risk of any antibiotic, diarrhea, rash, hepatitis
  • Metronidazole: metallic taste, nausea, peripheral neuropathy (>4 weeks), encephalopathy/cerebellar signs, warfarin INR rises sharply, QT prolongation, alcohol intolerance (weak evidence)
  • Metronidazole has near-complete oral absorption – PO as good as IV

Monitoring / pearls

INR within 3–5 days if on warfarin with metronidazole. Stop clindamycin early if diarrhea and test for C. difficile.

C. difficile therapy and other agents

Oral vancomycin, fidaxomicin; colistin/polymyxin and newer agents (ID only)
CoversC. difficile (oral vancomycin, fidaxomicin – act in the gut lumen, not absorbed)
Does not coverOral vancomycin and fidaxomicin treat nothing outside the gut

When to use

  • First episode C. difficile → fidaxomicin (preferred, fewer recurrences) or oral vancomycin, 10 days
  • Fulminant (hypotension, ileus, megacolon) → vancomycin 500 mg PO/NG QID + metronidazole 500 mg IV q8h ± rectal vancomycin; surgery consult
  • Recurrence → fidaxomicin or vancomycin taper/pulse; consider fecal microbiota transplant after 2nd recurrence
  • Stop unnecessary antibiotics and PPIs; contact precautions
  • Colistin, cefiderocol, ceftazidime-avibactam, ceftolozane-tazobactam, meropenem-vaborbactam: CRE/MDR gram-negatives – ID approval

Usual adult doses

AgentUsual dose (normal renal function)Renal adjust?
Vancomycin PO125 mg PO QID ×10 days; fulminant 500 mg PO/NG QIDNo
Fidaxomicin200 mg PO BID ×10 days (extended-pulsed regimens for recurrence)No
Metronidazole IV (fulminant add-on)500 mg IV q8hNo

Side effects and interactions

  • Oral vancomycin/fidaxomicin: few systemic effects; nausea
  • Colistin: nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity

Monitoring / pearls

Do not test for cure. Do not treat colonization (no diarrhea). Bezlotoxumab is no longer available.

Practical: allergy, IV to PO, renal dosing

Applies across classes

Penicillin allergy

  • Most labelled patients (~90%+) are not allergic. PEN-FAST: Five years or less since reaction (2), Anaphylaxis/angioedema (2) or Severe cutaneous reaction (SJS/TEN/DRESS, 2), Treatment needed (1). Score <3 = low risk → direct oral amoxicillin challenge is reasonable.
  • Cephalosporins after penicillin allergy: ~1–2% cross-reactivity, mostly via shared side chains. Cefazolin has a unique side chain – usually safe. Carbapenems <1%. Aztreonam: avoid only with ceftazidime allergy.
  • True severe delayed reaction (SJS/TEN, DRESS) to any beta-lactam → avoid the class; ask ID/allergy.

IV to PO switch

  • Switch when: afebrile 24–48 h, hemodynamically stable, improving, gut working, a suitable oral drug exists. Not for: meningitis, endocarditis (unless POET-style criteria met), S. aureus bacteremia without ID input, severe neutropenia.
  • Near-100% oral bioavailability (no need for IV if absorbing): fluoroquinolones, linezolid, TMP-SMX, metronidazole, doxycycline/minocycline, clindamycin, rifampin, fluconazole.
  • Common step-downs: cefazolin → cephalexin; ceftriaxone → cefixime / amox-clav / TMP-SMX (by susceptibility); pip-tazo → amox-clav or cipro + metronidazole.

Renal dosing

  • Adjust for CrCl: most penicillins and cephalosporins (cefepime especially), carbapenems, aztreonam, fluoroquinolones (cipro, levo), vancomycin, aminoglycosides, daptomycin, TMP-SMX, clarithromycin, nitrofurantoin.
  • No renal adjustment: ceftriaxone, cloxacillin, doxycycline, minocycline, linezolid, clindamycin, metronidazole, azithromycin, moxifloxacin, rifampin, oral vancomycin, fidaxomicin.
  • Give a full first dose regardless of kidney function, then adjust.

Who covers what (quick)

NeedOptions
PseudomonasPip-tazo, cefepime, ceftazidime, meropenem/imipenem, aztreonam, ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin, aminoglycosides
MRSAVancomycin, linezolid, daptomycin (not lung), ceftaroline, TMP-SMX, doxycycline (SSTI), clindamycin (if D-test negative)
AnaerobesMetronidazole, amox-clav, pip-tazo, carbapenems, clindamycin (above diaphragm), moxifloxacin
AtypicalsAzithromycin, clarithromycin, doxycycline, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin
ESBLCarbapenems (ertapenem, meropenem); cystitis: nitrofurantoin, fosfomycin; by susceptibility: TMP-SMX, ciprofloxacin, aminoglycosides
EnterococcusAmpicillin/amoxicillin (E. faecalis), vancomycin; VRE: linezolid, daptomycin. Cephalosporins never cover enterococcus
